records.sourceFile: The Impact of Localized Muscle Mass on Sprint Mechanics During the Swing and Stance Phases of Division I Collegiate American Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Metoyer CJ, Lever JR, McGinty M, Landow L, Hunt R, Hauenstein JD, Huebner A, Stone MH, Wagle JP. The Impact of Localized Muscle Mass on Sprint Mechanics During the Swing and Stance Phases of Division I Collegiate American Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(9):959-963.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined how MRI-measured lower-extremity muscle volumes related to sprint swing and stance times across three position groups of Division I football players.
paper.tldr: Localized muscle-volume relationships with sprint phase times differed among Skills, Mids, and Bigs. The findings support position-specific profiling questions, but they do not show that selectively increasing or limiting one muscle will improve speed.
paper.methods: One hundred eight male Division I football players were classified as Skills, Mids, or Bigs. Lower-extremity muscle volumes were quantified with MRI, maximal-sprint stance and swing times were captured with inertial sensors, and stepwise multiple regressions were conducted separately within each position group.
paper.findings: Different muscle volumes were associated with shorter or longer swing and stance times in each position group. For example, greater vastus intermedius and sartorius volume related to shorter swing time in Skills, while other quadriceps, hamstring, hip, and lower-leg associations varied across Mids and Bigs. No single muscle profile generalized across positions.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional regressions cannot establish training causality and may overfit correlated muscle measures. Testing occurred across multiple sites, involved one male collegiate program, and did not test longitudinal adaptation, change of direction, injury, or whether isolated muscle targeting improves performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Use body-composition and sprint-mechanics information to form position-specific hypotheses and select broader training priorities. Validate any proposed relationship through repeat sprint testing and training response rather than acting directly on one regression coefficient.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes understand that useful mass depends on role, distribution, force expression, and movement skill. Avoid labeling one muscle as good or bad from a cross-sectional association.
paper.rtp: These healthy-athlete associations are not clearance criteria. During reconditioning, prioritize restored capacity, sprint exposure, phase mechanics, symptoms, and position-specific task tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Association between collision sport career duration and gait performance in male collegiate student-athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Oldham JR, Lanois CJ, Caccese JB, Crenshaw JR, Knight CA, Berkstresser B, Wang F, Howell DR, Meehan WP III, Buckley TA. Association Between Collision Sport Career Duration and Gait Performance in Male Collegiate Student-Athletes. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;50(9):2526-2533.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study tested whether longer collision-sport career duration was associated with poorer single- or dual-task gait in male collegiate athletes.
paper.tldr: Among 168 male collegiate collision-sport athletes, career duration was not associated with gait, cognitive accuracy, or dual-task cost. The null findings apply to healthy young men and do not establish that cumulative head impacts are harmless or predict later-life outcomes.
paper.methods: Male football, lacrosse, ice hockey, and wrestling athletes completed preseason instrumented single- and dual-task walking. Gait speed, stride length, working-memory accuracy, and dual-task costs were related to self-reported collision-sport career duration using linear regression.
paper.findings: Career duration was not significantly associated with single-task gait speed, beta -0.004, P=.35, or dual-task gait speed, beta -0.003, P=.57. Stride length, cognitive accuracy, and motor or cognitive dual-task costs were also not significantly associated with career duration.
paper.limitations: Exposure duration and continuity were self-reported, actual head-impact dose and sport rule differences were unavailable, and the study included only healthy college-aged men. Cross-sectional clinical gait testing may miss subtle or later-emerging effects.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use years played alone or a normal gait test as a cumulative-brain-health verdict. Maintain exposure reduction, symptom reporting, concussion care, and longitudinal multimodal assessment.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that a null group result is reassuring only for the measured tasks and age range. Encourage honest symptom reporting and long-term brain-health habits without using career duration to frighten or falsely reassure athletes.
paper.rtp: Instrumented gait can contribute to concussion assessment, but this study does not validate it as a stand-alone clearance test or cumulative-exposure screen.

records.sourceFile: Feedback of GPS training data within professional English soccer A comparison of decision making and perceptions between coaches players and (1).pdf

paper.citation: Nosek P, Brownlee TE, Drust B, Andrew M. Feedback of GPS Training Data Within Professional English Soccer: A Comparison of Decision Making and Perceptions Between Coaches, Players and Performance Staff. Science and Medicine in Football. 2021;5(1):35-47.
paper.abstract: This survey study compared how professional-soccer coaches, players, and performance staff perceived GPS training feedback, decision value, barriers, and preferred delivery.
paper.tldr: Professional-soccer stakeholders valued GPS feedback but wanted different information and delivery. Too much data, poor communication, and no shared purpose reduced usefulness, making report design and conversation as important as metric collection.
paper.methods: An online convenience survey was completed by 176 coaches, players, and performance staff working in professional soccer. Questions covered the importance of data to reflection and decision making, desired variables, barriers to use, behavior-change perceptions, and player delivery preferences.
paper.findings: All groups rated training data as at least somewhat important. Coaches most wanted high-intensity actions and work-rate information; players preferred total distance, high-speed running, and sprint distance and commonly favored messages or changing-room displays. Information volume, communication, and lack of a common goal emerged as barriers.
paper.limitations: The convenience sample was small relative to professional soccer, could include clustered responses from the same clubs, and measured perceptions rather than observed decisions or performance. The findings concerned GPS and do not automatically transfer to other monitoring systems.
paper.practicalImplications: Define the decision and audience before sending data. Use a small metric set, shared language, appropriate timing, and a clear action or reflection prompt; evaluate whether feedback changes understanding and behavior.
paper.athleteDev: Give athletes concise, role-relevant feedback and invite interpretation rather than sending unexplained numbers. Athlete input on timing, format, and usefulness should be part of the monitoring process.
paper.rtp: Return-to-sport dashboards should communicate the current question, comparison, uncertainty, and next action. More GPS variables do not make a clearance decision stronger without clinical and functional context.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring injury occurrence in elite soccer players   after preseason strength training with eccentric overload.pdf

paper.citation: Askling C, Karlsson J, Thorstensson A. Hamstring Injury Occurrence in Elite Soccer Players After Preseason Strength Training With Eccentric Overload. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports. 2003;13(4):244-250.
paper.abstract: This randomized trial evaluated whether additional preseason flywheel hamstring training affected hamstring injury occurrence, strength, and sprint speed in elite male soccer players.
paper.tldr: Ten weeks of additional concentric-eccentric flywheel hamstring training was followed by fewer injured players, 3 of 15 versus 10 of 15, plus strength and sprint gains. The small trial and unusually high control injury rate limit the precision and portability of the effect.
paper.methods: Thirty elite male players from two Swedish teams were randomized to ordinary training or 16 additional hamstring sessions over 10 weeks. The intervention used bilateral knee flexion on a flywheel device with eccentric overload. Isokinetic strength and maximal running speed were tested, and hamstring injuries were recorded over 10 months.
paper.findings: Hamstring injuries occurred in 3 of 15 training-group players and 10 of 15 controls. The intervention group significantly improved concentric and eccentric hamstring strength and maximal running speed, but performance changes were not clearly coupled to individual injury occurrence.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and unblinded, detailed football exposure was not recorded, team personnel registered injuries, and control-group injury occurrence was unusually high. The combined flywheel protocol does not isolate an exercise, dose, or mechanism.
paper.practicalImplications: Include progressive eccentric-overload hamstring work during preseason, but treat it as one component of preparation. Monitor tolerance and combine it with sprint exposure, total loading, availability, and ongoing injury surveillance.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes why hamstring capacity and high-speed exposure are developed progressively. Build technique and adherence without implying that completing one exercise eliminates injury risk.
paper.rtp: Eccentric hamstring work can support reconditioning, but return requires restored strength, sprint exposure, symptoms, confidence, and sport-specific tolerance rather than completion of a flywheel protocol alone.

records.sourceFile: How does the workload applied during the training week and the contextual factors affect the physical responses of professional soccer players in the match.pdf

paper.citation: Guerrero-Calderón B, Klemp M, Morcillo JA, Memmert D. How Does the Workload Applied During the Training Week and the Contextual Factors Affect the Physical Responses of Professional Soccer Players in the Match? International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching. 2021;16(4):994-1003.
paper.abstract: This season-long observational study modeled how weekly GPS training load and contextual factors related to subsequent match-running output in two professional soccer teams.
paper.tldr: Weekly training and match context explained substantial variation in professional-soccer running output. Higher weekly high-intensity distance related positively and total distance negatively to match output, but the observational models are local planning evidence rather than a causal microcycle formula.
paper.methods: GPS training and match records from Spanish first- and second-division teams were analyzed across a season using linear mixed models. Weekly total, high-intensity, and sprint distance were related to match outputs while accounting for player, position, season period, division, opposition quality, and formation.
paper.findings: Conditional R-squared values were 0.51 for match total distance, 0.58 for high-intensity running, and 0.60 for sprint distance. Weekly total distance had a negative relationship with match output, high-intensity distance had a positive relationship, and position, season period, division, and opposition quality contributed context.
paper.limitations: The two-team observational design cannot establish that changing weekly load causes the predicted match response. Results depend on GPS thresholds and model choices and did not fully represent tactical, technical, internal-load, wellness, or availability factors.
paper.practicalImplications: Build team-specific models and review high-intensity exposure alongside total volume and match context. Use estimates to support, not dictate, microcycle decisions and monitor whether changes improve availability and match preparation.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why similar weekly totals can contain different intensity and recovery demands. Use individual trends and role requirements to help athletes understand the purpose of each exposure.
paper.rtp: A returning player's weekly load should be progressed against individual tolerance and planned match demands. Group associations do not provide clearance thresholds or justify rapid high-intensity escalation.

records.sourceFile: Cannabis use and sport - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Docter S, Khan M, Gohal C, Ravi B, Bhandari M, Gandhi R, Leroux T. Cannabis Use and Sport: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2020;12(2):189-199.
paper.abstract: This systematic review synthesized athlete cannabis-use prevalence, evidence on performance and recovery, and sport-policy variation.
paper.tldr: About 23.4% of respondents across 11 athlete studies reported past-year cannabis use, but performance evidence was sparse and inconsistent and no direct recovery evidence was found. Cannabis, THC, and CBD should not be presented as interchangeable or proven recovery tools.
paper.methods: PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase were searched through November 2018, supplemented by sport policies and official documents. Thirty-seven studies were included; 11 prevalence studies represented 46,202 respondents, and most research was cross-sectional in elite or university athletes.
paper.findings: Approximately 23.4% of athletes reported cannabis use in the prior 12 months. Two studies reported negative performance effects and two reported no effect. No eligible study directly assessed athletic recovery, and sport organizations varied widely in urine THC thresholds and sanctions at the time of review.
paper.limitations: Evidence was primarily level-4, self-reported, and heterogeneous in athlete population, product, cannabinoid, dose, timing, and outcome. Recovery evidence was absent, and regulations summarized in 2020 may no longer be current.
paper.practicalImplications: Use confidential, nonjudgmental screening and distinguish THC, CBD, route, dose, timing, product quality, and current anti-doping policy. Do not recommend cannabis for recovery based on this evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Build substance and product literacy, including impairment, contamination, legal, and anti-doping risks. Make help-seeking easier than concealment and avoid assuming use means misuse.
paper.rtp: Cannabis should not be used to mask pain, sleep difficulty, or anxiety during return to sport. Symptoms and use disclosures may require medical assessment, but use history alone is not a clearance decision.

records.sourceFile: Cardiovascular Health of Retired    Field-Based Athletes A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: McHugh C, Hind K, Davey D, Wilson F. Cardiovascular Health of Retired Field-Based Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;7(8):2325967119862750.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated cardiovascular risk factors and subclinical disease in retired male football and soccer athletes.
paper.tldr: Retired football and soccer athletes had a mixed cardiovascular profile rather than durable protection from prior sport. Higher body mass and lineman history identified greater concern, supporting structured health transition and long-term screening.
paper.methods: Thirteen studies included 4,350 retired male field-sport athletes aged approximately 42 to 66 years, and eight studies included controls. Cardiovascular risk factors, coronary calcium, carotid plaque, and position-related findings were reviewed with methodological-quality assessment and random-effects analysis where possible.
paper.findings: Four of six studies reported higher systolic blood pressure in retired athletes, about half reported higher HDL, about 80% lower triglycerides, and all reporting LDL comparisons found higher LDL. Coronary calcium and carotid plaque were similar to controls, while retired linemen had roughly twice the cardiometabolic-syndrome prevalence of nonlinemen.
paper.limitations: Definitions and reporting were inconsistent, observational studies were vulnerable to selection, survivor, body-mass, and lifestyle confounding, and only male football and soccer athletes were represented. The evidence did not support one pooled retired-athlete risk estimate.
paper.practicalImplications: Create a transition pathway that preserves activity and follows blood pressure, lipids, body composition, symptoms, sleep, and primary care after sport. Give added attention to athletes leaving high-body-mass roles.
paper.athleteDev: Prepare athletes for health after eligibility or retirement, including sustainable training, nutrition, medical follow-up, identity transition, and social support. Prior fitness is not permanent protection.
paper.rtp: This review concerns long-term health rather than injury clearance. Cardiovascular symptoms or abnormal screening during return to activity require clinician-led evaluation and individualized exercise decisions.

records.sourceFile: Clinical risk factors for Achilles   tendinopathy- a systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: van der Vlist AC, Breda SJ, Oei EHG, Verhaar JAN, de Vos RJ. Clinical Risk Factors for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(21):1352-1361.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated longitudinal clinical factors associated with the development of Achilles tendinopathy.
paper.tldr: Ten high-risk-of-bias cohort studies provided only limited evidence for nine possible Achilles-tendinopathy risk factors, while 26 commonly proposed factors were not associated. The review does not support a universal screening score.
paper.methods: Five databases were searched through February 2018 for human cohort studies of clinical risk factors. Ten cohorts were retained from 5,111 records. Imaging-only factors were excluded, risk of bias was assessed, and heterogeneity prevented quantitative pooling.
paper.findings: Limited evidence implicated prior lower-limb tendinopathy or fracture, ofloxacin exposure, cold-weather training, reduced plantar-flexor strength, selected gait features, moderate alcohol use, and renal or transplant-related factors. Overweight, static foot posture, physical activity level, and 23 other proposed factors were not associated.
paper.limitations: Every included study had high risk of bias, definitions and populations were heterogeneous, only English-language publications were selected, and several signals arose from nonathlete medical populations. No causal effect or validated multivariable prediction rule was established.
paper.practicalImplications: Prioritize history, symptoms, recent exposure, plantar-flexor capacity, medication, and medical context. Avoid using static posture, body mass, or an isolated screening measure as proof of future tendinopathy.
paper.athleteDev: Teach progressive calf and tendon loading, recovery, and early symptom reporting. Frame risk as modifiable context and capacity rather than a fixed label.
paper.rtp: Return decisions should follow symptoms, tendon loading tolerance, calf capacity, running and jumping exposure, and sport demands. The reviewed risk factors are not clearance thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Core body temperatures in intermittent sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Henderson MJ, Grandou C, Chrismas BCR, Coutts AJ, Impellizzeri FM, Taylor L. Core Body Temperatures in Intermittent Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023;53(11):2147-2170.
paper.abstract: This systematic review characterized peak competition core temperatures reported in healthy adult intermittent-sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Most intermittent-sport studies observed competition hyperthermia: 24 of 34 reported peaks between 38.5 and 39.5 degrees Celsius and six reported at least 39.5 degrees. Heterogeneity prevents a universal threshold or one proven intervention.
paper.methods: Web of Science, MEDLINE, and SPORTDiscus were searched through April 2023. Thirty-four studies with at least 386 participants were included if core temperature was measured during competition without an intervention intended to alter heat strain. Methodological characteristics were evaluated and findings synthesized descriptively.
paper.findings: Four studies found no hyperthermia, 24 found modest hyperthermia with peak core temperature from 38.5 to 39.5 degrees Celsius, and six found marked hyperthermia at or above 39.5 degrees. Twenty-seven studies were observational, with the remainder experimental or quasi-experimental.
paper.limitations: Sports, competition duration, environment, athlete level, measurement method, and sampling schedule were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. Peak-temperature categories do not define individual illness, and intervention effectiveness was not evaluated.
paper.practicalImplications: Prepare heat-acclimation, cooling, hydration, substitution, monitoring, and emergency plans for intermittent competition. Interpret temperature with symptoms, environment, workload, medical risk, and individual response.
paper.athleteDev: Rehearse heat strategies and teach early symptom reporting. Athletes should understand that high strain can occur even when the sport includes breaks and that tolerance is not permission to ignore warning signs.
paper.rtp: Progress environmental exposure alongside sport load after illness, injury, or heat intolerance. Core temperature alone is not a return criterion; medical history and symptom response remain central.

records.sourceFile: Current Evidence for the Use of Jugular Vein Compression Collars in Sport - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Delgadillo BE, Montz F, Ward B Jr, Herson AB, Toldi JP. Current Evidence for the Use of Jugular Vein Compression Collars in Sport: A Systematic Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(1):18-27.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated whether external jugular-vein compression collars reduce concussion or head-impact-related brain changes in high-impact sports and tactical activity.
paper.tldr: Fifteen collar studies reported favorable selected imaging, neurocognitive, vascular, and pulse-pressure signals, but concussion incidence did not differ. Visible devices, team-level randomization, adolescent samples, and substantial manufacturer-linked evidence prevent a prevention claim.
paper.methods: A multiple-database search through June 2024 identified 15 studies of jugular compression collars, including randomized trials and prospective analyses in sport and tactical settings. Outcomes included white-matter imaging, neurocognitive testing, vascular measures, pulse pressure, head impacts, and concussion incidence.
paper.findings: Collar groups showed less alteration in selected white-matter measures, favorable short-term neurocognitive findings, larger internal jugular and smaller internal carotid cross-sectional area, and moderated peak pulse pressure. No significant concussion-incidence difference was established.
paper.limitations: Most evidence involved adolescents, randomization was commonly by team, participants and observers could see collar assignment, and off-season impacts were not controlled. The Q-Collar inventor advised the company that funded most included studies, creating a material conflict-of-interest concern.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not substitute a collar for established concussion prevention, exposure management, recognition, removal, and clinical care. Treat surrogate imaging and short-term findings as preliminary until independent trials demonstrate meaningful clinical benefit.
paper.athleteDev: Explain the difference between a biomarker change and proven protection. Equipment should never encourage riskier contact behavior or reduced symptom reporting.
paper.rtp: Jugular compression collars do not prevent the need for concussion assessment or alter return-to-sport progression. They are not clearance or treatment devices based on current evidence.

records.sourceFile: Dehydration Impairs Cognitive Performance- A Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Wittbrodt MT, Millard-Stafford M. Dehydration Impairs Cognitive Performance: A Meta-analysis. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018;50(11):2360-2368.
paper.abstract: This meta-analysis quantified how dehydration magnitude related to cognitive performance across different tasks and experimental protocols.
paper.tldr: Dehydration produced a small overall cognitive decrement, with larger effects for attention, motor coordination, and executive function and above 2% body-mass loss. The 2% comparison is a group pattern, not a universal athlete threshold.
paper.methods: Thirty-three studies provided 280 effect estimates from 413 participants with 1% to 6% body-mass loss. Standardized mean differences were pooled with multivariate meta-analysis, and cognitive domain, outcome type, dehydration magnitude, and study-design moderators were examined.
paper.findings: The overall effect was -0.21, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.11. Attention was -0.52, motor coordination -0.40, and executive function -0.24. Effects were larger above 2% body-mass loss, -0.28, than at or below 2%, -0.14, while reaction-time-specific tasks were not significantly impaired.
paper.limitations: Dehydration methods, heat and exercise exposure, cognitive tests, outcome definitions, and samples varied with significant heterogeneity. Mood, thirst, and effort may contribute, and many samples were small and convenient; subgroup results do not establish an individual cutoff.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect hydration before decision-heavy practice and competition, especially in heat, and monitor individual fluid loss and response. Use body-mass change as context rather than a rigid cognitive-performance threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to start hydrated, use rehearsed fluid plans, and recognize concentration, mood, coordination, and heat symptoms. Avoid both underdrinking and forced overdrinking.
paper.rtp: Correct dehydration during illness or reconditioning, but do not interpret rehydration alone as restored readiness. Symptoms, medical status, and progressive task tolerance still govern return.

records.sourceFile: Do multi-ingredient protein supplements augment resistance training-induced gains in skeletal muscle mass and strength - A systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 trials.pdf

paper.citation: O'Bryan KR, Doering TM, Morton RW, Coffey VG, Phillips SM, Cox GR. Do Multi-ingredient Protein Supplements Augment Resistance Training-induced Gains in Skeletal Muscle Mass and Strength? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of 35 Trials. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;54(10):573-581.
paper.abstract: This meta-analysis compared multi-ingredient protein supplementation with placebo, other non-multi-ingredient conditions, and protein-only supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training.
paper.tldr: Multi-ingredient protein products improved pooled fat-free mass and strength versus all non-multi-ingredient conditions, but they were not superior to protein alone. Training, adequate protein, safety, and cost remain the first decisions.
paper.methods: Thirty-five randomized resistance-training trials lasting at least six weeks included 1,387 participants. Random-effects analyses pooled fat-free mass, fat mass, and upper- and lower-body one-repetition maximum strength, with subgroup analyses by training status and age.
paper.findings: Versus all non-multi-ingredient conditions, multi-ingredient supplementation favored fat-free mass by 0.80 kg, lower-body one-repetition maximum by 4.22 kg, and upper-body one-repetition maximum by 2.56 kg. Benefits appeared larger in untrained and older groups, but direct comparisons showed no superiority to protein-only supplementation.
paper.limitations: Only retrievable English-language trials were included, ingredients and comparators varied, and moderate heterogeneity remained. Pooling placebo and active controls can magnify the apparent blend effect, and product-specific results do not generalize to every formulation.
paper.practicalImplications: First ensure sufficient energy, total protein, meal distribution, and progressive resistance training. If a multi-ingredient product is considered, compare it with a simpler protein option and verify dose, safety, third-party testing, cost, and athlete need.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to evaluate the full ingredient list and evidence rather than assuming more ingredients means more adaptation. Supplements should fill a defined need within a sound nutrition plan.
paper.rtp: Protein supplementation may help meet rehabilitation nutrition targets, but a blend does not replace progressive loading or demonstrate readiness. Coordinate use with nutrition and medical staff.
